extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in the history and practical development of early steam locomotives (engineers, historians, technically-curious general public)
extracted.subtask_description: Historical-technical guidance and implicit evaluation criteria for early steam locomotive design and railway practice, derived from nineteenth-century experiments and failures (Trevithick, Blenkinsop, Blackett, Hedley, Stephenson). Emphasises practical mechanical, boiler, traction, and operational considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhesion via engine weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficient adhesion between smooth wheels and smooth rails can be achieved by the weight of the engine itself, making rack-rails, toothed wheels, endless chains, or legged mechanisms unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: William Hedley's experiments (weighted frame with windlasses) demonstrated the proportion of power to weight needed so smooth wheels would not slip; successive experiments showed a weighted engine could draw required loads in varied weather. Anti-pattern: assuming adhesion is impossible and therefore adopting complex mechanical alternatives (rack, chain, legs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rail/road strength must match locomotive weight
rubrics_metrics.description: The existing tramway/rails must be capable of supporting the much greater weight of locomotives; otherwise rails or tram-plates will break and operations fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trevithick's and Wylam experiences: heavy locomotives frequently broke tram-plates or ran off the road when rails were too light. Remedy: reconstruct road with heavier rails/plates before introducing heavy locomotives; otherwise the locomotive may be unusable or cause frequent breakdowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waste-steam handling to reduce nuisance and interruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Directly exhausting high-pressure waste steam into the open can cause loud blasts that frighten animals and disrupt operation; a reservoir behind the chimney to receive waste steam can allow gradual, quieter release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At Wylam, locomotives initially had waste steam blown into the air, stopping for passing horses; solution was a reservoir behind the chimney into which waste steam was thrown and from which it escaped quietly. Implement steam-capture or muffling measures to avoid social/operational nuisance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaust-jet (blast) increases draught and combustion
rubrics_metrics.description: Directing exhaust steam into the chimney can increase draught, quicken combustion, and thereby increase engine power (the steam-blast principle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trevithick initially routed waste steam into the chimney without exploiting the blast effect; later developments recognized the blast's value in increasing draught. Design should consider using exhaust to augment furnace draught rather than merely to dispose of steam; anti-pattern: ignoring blast and relying on bellows or manual fanners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase heating surface (boiler/flue design) for more power
rubrics_metrics.description: Boiler designs that increase heating surface (for example, returning the flue through the boiler) yield greater power by improving steam generation efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wylam improved heating surface by returning the flue through a wrought-iron boiler, resulting in increased power. Design boilers with sufficient heating surface area and effective flue routing to match expected loads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple (double) cylinders for improved operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Using two cylinders (double cylinder) rather than a single cylinder provides smoother and more effective motion for locomotives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blenkinsop's engines (invention of the double cylinder by Matthew Murray) used two cylinders with cranks at right angles driving two pinions, improving working characteristics. Consider multi-cylinder arrangements to avoid dead-centre problems and improve torque delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of flywheel to carry crank over dead points
rubrics_metrics.description: A flywheel can secure rotatory motion and carry the crank through dead points between piston strokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trevithick and other early engines incorporated a flywheel at one side to provide rotatory momentum and ensure the crank moves past dead points. Include adequate flywheel/mass-inertia in transmission design where single-cylinder configurations are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roughening wheel periphery as adhesion contingency
rubrics_metrics.description: Where adhesion is a concern, roughening the driving-wheel periphery (bolts, cross-grooves) can be used to obtain better bite on the rail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trevithick's patent provided that wheel peripheries could be made rough by projection of bolts or cross-grooves. This is an engineering option if weight-based adhesion is insufficient, but may increase rail wear; use only as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanically complex traction schemes when simpler adhesion suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: Schemes such as rack-and-pinion rails, endless chains, or legged 'walking' mechanisms add friction, complexity, cost, and maintenance burden and often proved impractical compared to adhesion-based locomotives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Blenkinsop's rack-rail (worked but cumbersome), Chapman's chain-driven scheme (friction, expensive to maintain), Brunton's legged machine (experimental and dangerous). Prefer simpler adhesion-based solutions once adhesion via weight is demonstrated; weigh complexity vs. practical maintainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety design and reliable pressure controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Boiler safety valves and pressure controls must be properly designed and not overloaded; incorrect handling can lead to catastrophic boiler explosions with fatalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brunton's Mechanical Traveller suffered a boiler burst when the driver overloaded the safety valve, causing deaths and injuries. Include fail-safe safety valves, clear operating procedures, and protection against tampering/overpressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit terrain: self-acting inclines and gravity haulage
rubrics_metrics.description: Where geography permits, self-acting inclines using descending loaded wagons to draw up empty ones by rope are an economical means of haulage and should be used to reduce horse or locomotive labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stephenson laid down self-acting inclines at Killingworth and Willington to economise haulage. Use incline systems for suitable slopes to reduce motive power requirements on level sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for durability, ease of maintenance, and constant attention reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Early experimental locomotives frequently required constant attention and were 'under repair as often as at work'; designs should prioritise robustness and maintainability to deliver reliable commercial service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackett's and other early engines suffered constant breakdowns (plugs, pumps, cranks); procuring competent mechanics and designing simpler, more robust mechanisms reduced downtime. Antipattern: overly complicated assemblies that demand constant tinkering.
